Theory of the 1/91/9 Magnetization Plateau of the Spin-1/21/2 Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet

Pratyay Ghosh Email: pratyay.ghosh@epfl.ch Affiliation: Institute of Physics, Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Frédéric Mila Affiliation: Institute of Physics, Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract

We investigate the 1/91/9 magnetization plateau of the spin-1/21/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet using infinite projected entangled-pair states and identify a spin-density-wave state with a 2727-site unit cell and a lower variational energy than previous approaches. In contrast to higher-magnetization plateaus, which are well described by localized magnons on nonoverlapping hexagons and preserve a sixfold rotational symmetry, the 1/91/9 plateau only keeps a threefold rotational symmmetry and consists of a tiling by three types of 99-site clusters related by ±2π/3\pm 2\pi/3 rotations. These conclusions are supported by a complementary cluster mean-field theory which correctly preserves the symmetry of the higher plateaus but leads to the same spontaneous symmetry breaking for the 1/91/9 plateau with a qualitatively similar pattern of nine different local magnetizations.

The spin-1/21/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet (KHA) is a paradigmatic example of a frustrated quantum magnet, in which strong frustration and quantum fluctuations suppress conventional magnetic order and produce a dense manifold of low-energy states [8, 33, 34, 36], making it one of the most intensively studied systems in quantum magnetism. The nature of its ground state remains under debate, with leading theoretical proposals including quantum spin liquids (QSLs) with fractionalized excitations and valence-bond crystals (VBCs) [38, 49, 53, 11, 29, 7, 58, 35, 9].The application of a magnetic field further enriches the phase diagram, as the magnetization exhibits a sequence of fractional plateaus that signal distinct field-induced quantum phases [52, 43, 1, 39, 27, 47, 60, 5, 44, 59, 13, 26, 37, 32, 28, 54, 25, 6, 12, 48, 10]. The higher-field plateaus at m/ms=1/3m/m_{s}=1/3, 5/95/9, and 7/97/9, where msm_{s} denotes the saturation magnetization, are relatively well understood. In contrast, the microscopic nature of the low-field 1/91/9 plateau remains unresolved and is the subject of ongoing debate.

High-field measurements conducted in 2024 on yttrium-based hydroxyhalide kagome antiferromagnets confirmed the presence of a 1/91/9 magnetization plateau [28, 54, 62, 61, 24]. A 1/91/9 magnetization plateau has also been reported recently in Y-kapellasite [3]. Further experimental evidence for plateau-like behavior has emerged from high-field measurements of the titanium-based kagome family Cs8​AB3​Ti12​F48{}{}{}{}\mathrm{Cs}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{8}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{8}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{AB}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{3}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{Ti}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{12}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{12}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{F}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{48}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{48}}\mathrm{}} (A = Rb, Li; B = K, Na) [4]; both Cs8​RbK3​Ti12​F48{}{}{}{}\mathrm{Cs}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{8}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{8}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{RbK}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{3}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{Ti}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{12}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{12}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{F}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{48}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{48}}\mathrm{}} and Cs8​LiK3​Ti12​F48{}{}{}{}\mathrm{Cs}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{8}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{8}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{LiK}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{3}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{Ti}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{12}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{12}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{F}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{48}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{48}}\mathrm{}} exhibit robust 1/91/9 plateau-like phases, despite the absence of the typically more prominent 1/31/3 plateau. In contrast, Cs8​LiNa3​Ti12​F48{}{}{}{}\mathrm{Cs}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{8}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{8}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{LiNa}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{3}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{Ti}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{12}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{12}}\mathrm{}}\mathrm{F}{\vphantom{\mathrm{X}}}_{\vphantom{\mathrm{2}}\smash[t]{\mathrm{48}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\mathrm{2}}}\hphantom{\mathrm{48}}\mathrm{}} displays suppression of both the 1/91/9 feature and the quantum-disordered zero-field ground state. These findings indicate that the 1/91/9 plateau is sensitive to the underlying frustrated exchange network. In the ideal KHA, the higher-field 1/31/3, 5/95/9, and 7/97/9 plateaus are attributed to localized magnons [50, 51]. Bond anisotropies disrupt this mechanism by introducing dispersion to the localized magnons, which can suppress these plateaus. The persistence of the 1/91/9 plateau in titanium-based compounds, despite deviations from the ideal kagome model [4], suggests the presence of a qualitatively different mechanism that is more robust against bond anisotropies. However, the microscopic state responsible for this plateau remains unresolved. Theoretical studies of the ideal spin-1/21/2 KHA propose several competing states: a topological ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} QSL [39, 26], VBCs with 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} [47, 13, 12] or 3×33\times 3 periodicity [6, 48], and a spin-density-wave (SDW) state [10].

In this Letter, we investigate the 1/91/9 magnetization plateau of the spin-1/21/2 KHA using infinite projected entangled-pair states (iPEPS) [30, 31, 57, 56, 22] and the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG) [40, 45, 15, 41, 18]. Extending previous tensor network studies, which were restricted to 99-site unit cells [47, 13, 12], we consider a 2727-site unit cell. Our results demonstrate that the 1/91/9 plateau is stabilized over a finite range of applied magnetic fields. We identify the underlying state as an SDW with a 2727-site unit cell composed of three types of 99-site clusters related by successive 2​π/32\pi/3 rotations. This structure breaks the sixfold rotational symmetry of all hexagons and only keeps three inequivalent centers of threefold rotation. Both the nearest-neighbor (NN) spin correlations and the local magnetizations display spatial modulation, with nine different local magnetizations. A complementary cluster mean-field theory (CMFT) analysis reveals the same spontaneous breaking of sixfold rotational symmetry and produces a qualitatively consistent magnetization pattern.

Previous tensor network studies employed 99-site unit cells, which represent the minimum size compatible with the 1/91/9 magnetization state [26, 47, 13, 12]. The variational energies obtained in these studies are comparable to those of the proposed ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} QSL. [39]. More recent calculations utilizing resonating-valence-bond (RVB) wave functions [6] and neural-network quantum states (NQS) [48] have achieved lower energies with a 2727-site unit cell. These finite-system results, particularly the size-dependent outcomes observed in NQS, motivate an investigation of the 1/91/9 plateau in the thermodynamic limit. The present study examines infinite systems with 2727-site variational unit cells, referred to as the 2727-site ansatz, utilizing the tensor constructions shown in Fig. 1(a). A 3636-site unit cell construction was also considered; however, stabilization of the 1/91/9 plateau could not be achieved within this ansatz. The tensor network representing the 2727-site ansatz consists of three six-site and three three-site coarse-grained tensors. The size of the variational unit cell does not determine the periodicity of the state; larger cells can accommodate both smaller-period states and structures with periods up to the chosen size. These constructions enable the examination of spatial structures proposed in earlier studies. In this construction, the tensors form a honeycomb lattice connected by virtual bonds of dimension DD, allowing for analysis of the infinite two-dimensional environment using the hexagonal CTMRG scheme [42, 15, 41, 18].

Due to the high computational cost associated with full-update [31, 46] and automatic-differentiation [23] optimizations for enlarged unit cells, we employ simple update [30] to access larger bond dimensions. Since our primary focus is on the magnetization plateau, which is expected to be gapped, the simple-update approximation is expected to capture its essential physics. The resulting infinite tensor networks are contracted using the hexagonal CTMRG environment, which consists of three corner tensors CC and six edge tensors TT [see Fig. 1(b)]. The auxiliary dimension χ\chi determines the accuracy of the approximate contraction. We verify convergence of energy and magnetization with respect to χ\chi. Initial optimization with a six-tensor unit cell produces states that approximately preserve threefold rotational symmetry about the center across the entire field range studied. By exploiting this symmetry, a reduced two-tensor representation is employed in subsequent calculations [15, 18], thereby improving numerical convergence while preserving the structure of the optimized state.

In the presence of a magnetic field, the Hamiltonian includes a Zeeman term, −h∑iSiz-h\sum_{i}S_{i}^{z}. The field hh is expressed in units of the nearest-neighbor (NN) exchange. Figure 2(a) presents magnetization curves derived from the 2727-site ansatz for various bond dimensions DD as a function of hh. The magnetization increases continuously from zero at zero field and attains the 1/91/9 plateau at h≃0.2h\simeq 0.2. This plateau persists up to h≃0.46h\simeq 0.46, after which the magnetization rises toward the 1/31/3 plateau, with a subtle feature near m/ms=5/27m/m_{s}=5/27. Figure 2(b) displays the energy e⁡(m)=e⁡(m,h)−h​me(m)=e(m,h)-hm of the m/ms=1/9m/m_{s}=1/9 state as a function of DD. At D≥12D\geq 12, the calculated energy is already lower than those obtained from both RVB wave-function ansatz [6] and NQS [48]. Extrapolation to large DD yields an even lower value [see also Tab. 1]. In contrast, previously reported energies for 99-site iPEPS and iPESS [13], as well as for the proposed ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} QSL state [26], are substantially higher 11 1 We exclude Ref. [10] from the quantitative comparison because its reported estimate of e⁡(m)e(m) for the 1/91/9 plateau is lower than established estimates of the zero-field KHA ground-state energy, including the value reported in their own previous work [9]. This discrepancy also appears to conflict with an exact lower bound on the zero-field energy [48], and its origin remains unclear.. Although the energy is not fully converged at the largest DD considered, its consistent decrease with increasing DD, along with the lower energy already achieved at D≥12D\geq 12, provides strong evidence supporting the state obtained with the 2727-site ansatz.

Figure 3(a) shows a representative example of local magnetizations and NN spin-spin correlations corresponding to the 1/91/9 plateau for h=0.4h=0.4 at D=15D=15. This state exhibits an SDW pattern with a 2727-site magnetic unit cell of the 3×33\times 3 type, which remains robust for D≥10D\geq 10. Our initial simulations use six independent tensors, allowing all 27 sites in the unit cell to evolve independently. However, since we observe an approximate threefold rotational symmetry about the center of the tensor network unit cell, we exploit this symmetry to reduce the number of independent sites from 27 to 9, thereby improving numerical convergence and obtaining a lower-energy state. The resulting state, thus, can be constructed from a 99-site triangular cluster by applying successive ∓2π/3\mp 2\pi/3 rotations about the center, combined with translations along the 𝐚1±𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{1}\pm\mathbf{a}_{2} directions, where 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{2} are the primitive lattice vectors. The state contains three inequivalent C3C_{3} rotation centers, indicated by filled markers in Figure 3(a). Although it shares certain similarities with the previously reported VBC states with a 2727-site unit cell [6, 48], our state exhibits different local magnetization patterns. Note that the states identified as VBCs in previous studies may also be interpreted as SDWs, given the pronounced spatial modulation of their local magnetizations. Like our state, the VBC reported in Ref. [6] and the two states referred to as VBC A and VBC B in Ref. [48] all feature three inequivalent C3C_{3} rotation centers, around which the spins exhibit alternating degrees of polarization. However, on the hexagon marked by the filled hexagon, all spins in our state are polarized along the applied field, whereas in the VBCs reported in Refs. [6, 48], the weakly polarized spins point opposite to the field. The distinction from VBC B in Ref. [48] also lies in the arrangement of strongly and weakly polarized spins around the three hexagons that contain the C3C_{3}-symmetric centers. In VBC B, these arrangements are equivalent around all three hexagons. In our state, however, the arrangement around the hexagon marked by the filled hexagon is reversed relative to those around the hexagons marked by the filled star and filled circle.

Although the 1/91/9 plateau exhibits a distinct structure as compared to higher plateaus, it can be approached from the localized-magnon picture. Starting from saturation, the 7/97/9, 5/95/9, and 1/31/3 plateaus correspond to localized one-, two-, and three-magnons on nonoverlapping hexagons [Fig. 3(c)]. The localization of these magnons maintains the sixfold rotational symmetry of each hexagon. Specifically, the 1/31/3 plateau may be interpreted as singlets (three-magnon states) on nonoverlapping hexagons, with all other spins remaining polarized [Fig. 3(c)]. One possible route to the 1/91/9 plateau is to demote these singlets to |t−⟩|t_{-}\rangle triplets with mz=−1m_{z}=-1. The central question is whether introducing these triplets leads to spontaneous breaking of the sixfold symmetry around the hexagons.

To evaluate this scenario, we perform CMFT analysis on clusters of three adjacent down-pointing elementary triangles, hereafter referred to as “supertriangles” [Fig. 3(b)]. Motivated by the iPEPS results, the lattice is tiled with copies of the cluster, each related by successive ∓2π/3\mp 2\pi/3 rotations about hexagon centers and translations along 𝐚1±𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{1}\pm\mathbf{a}_{2}. In this approach, each supertriangle is solved exactly within a fixed total-SzS^{z} sector, while intercluster couplings are treated through self-consistent boundary mean fields. Although the cluster Hamiltonian respects C3C_{3} and σ​’\sigma’ reflection symmetries, the CMFT solution is not constrained to preserve them and may exhibit additional symmetries in the full lattice state [Fig. 3(e)].

For the 7/97/9, 5/95/9, and 1/31/3 plateaus, the mean-field ground states retain C6C_{6} symmetry about the supertriangle centers and display only two distinct local magnetizations [55], consistent with localized-magnon states [Fig. 3(e)I]. In contrast, at m/ms=1/9m/m_{s}=1/9, the ground state spontaneously breaks the C6C_{6} symmetry [Fig. 3(e)IV] and results in nine distinct local magnetizations within the cluster [Fig. 3(b)]. Consequently, the state also breaks all reflection symmetries of the supertriangle [Fig. 3(e)IV]. The C3C_{3} symmetry about the centers indicated by filled symbols in Fig. 3(b) is preserved by construction. Although quantitative agreement with iPEPS is not expected at this level of approximation, the CMFT pattern replicates its key qualitative features: nine distinct local magnetizations and an identical relative arrangement of strongly polarized spins around the hexagons containing the C3C_{3} centers.

This qualitative agreement indicates that the |t−⟩|t_{-}\rangle states on the supertriangle hexagons reduce the system’s energy through spontaneous breaking of C6C_{6} symmetry, which redistributes spin polarization into the pattern depicted in Fig. 3(a). We emphasize that the iPEPS results are not fully converged with respect to DD, even at D=15D=15 [see Fig. 2(c)], so it remains possible that additional symmetries could be restored in the limit D→∞D\to\infty. Specifically, the weak breaking of the σ\sigma reflections passing through the hexagonal plaquette marked with a filled hexagon in Fig. 3(a) may vanish at larger DD, resulting in a state composed of supertriangles with the same symmetries as in Fig. 3(e)III. This scenario would reduce the number of independent local magnetizations from nine to six 22 2 In Ref. [48], additional symmetrization was imposed to obtain five independent magnetizations. Neither our numerical results nor our symmetry analysis provides evidence supporting this additional symmetrization.. Our finite-DD results cannot confirm or exclude this possibility [see Supplemental Material [55]]. Nevertheless, we find no indication of a restoration of all σ\sigma reflections while the σ′\sigma^{\prime} reflections remain broken, as in Fig. 3(e)II. Additionally, CMFT calculations using a 2727-site cluster [55] exhibit the same symmetry breaking and yield nine distinct local magnetizations. These findings suggest that the 1/91/9 plateau most likely exhibits nine distinct local magnetizations, although the possibility of six cannot be entirely ruled out.

In summary, the combination of iPEPS and CMFT leads to a consistent picture of the 1/91/9 magnetization plateau of the spin-1/21/2 KHA as a SDW that breaks sixfold rotational symmetry and consists of three 99-site clusters related by ±2π/3\pm 2\pi/3 rotations, resulting in a 27-site magnetic unit cell with nine distinct local magnetizations. An ideal technique to test this prediction is NMR, which provides a histogram of the local magnetizations, or some linear combinations if the nuclear spin is not on site, as in the 35Cl NMR investigation of Y-kapellasite [3]. Since the 1/91/9 plateau has been observed at fields of approximately 2020 T\mathrm{T} in yttrium-based hydroxyhalides, Y-kapellasite, and titanium-based kagome compounds at fields  [28, 54, 62, 61, 24, 3, 4], this prediction should be accessible to experimental verification. However, further theoretical studies of the spin-1/2 KHA with modified interactions are needed to clarify the microscopic origin of the robust 1/91/9 plateau-like phases and investigate the possible role of bond anisotropy [28, 54, 62, 61, 24, 3, 4]. A comparable analysis of the spin-11 KHA and related systems would also be interesting. In these systems, a gapped trimerized ground state has been identified [2, 20, 16], whereas no 1/91/9 plateau was observed in tensor network calculations with a 99-site unit cell [47]. Work is in progress along these lines.

At the technical level, the critical next step involves applying advanced tensor network optimization techniques, including full-update and automatic-differentiation methods, to the 2727-site ansatz, and more generally to enlarged-unit-cell ansatzes, to test ground-state structures with improved accuracy. It is therefore particularly valuable to develop strategies that enable these calculations at large bond dimensions. More broadly, our results demonstrate that tensor networks with enlarged unit cells, combined with hexagonal CTMRG, are effective for investigating phases with complex spatial structures. This methodology could also be extended to the maple-leaf lattice in a magnetic field [19, 21], where enlarged unit cells may facilitate access to exotic magnetization plateaus and field-induced states with spatial structures not captured in smaller-unit-cell calculations.

Supplemental Material for “Theory of the 1/91/9 Magnetization Plateau of the Spin-1/21/2 Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet”

I Infinite projected entangled pair states (iPEPS)

We use infinite projected entangled pair states (iPEPS) to approximate the ground states of the infinite kagome lattice. The iPEPS ansatz represents the many-body wave function as an infinite two-dimensional tensor network, with each tensor carrying one physical index and three virtual indices. The physical index has dimension d=2d=2 for spin-1/21/2 degrees of freedom, while the virtual indices have dimension DD, which controls the amount of entanglement that can be represented. All tensor-network calculations in this work were performed using the ITensor library [14].

To investigate the spatial structure of the magnetization plateau, we employ enlarged unit cells containing 27 kagome sites. The 27-site calculations are performed up to D=15D=15. The enlarged unit cells allow the tensors to develop spatially nonuniform patterns of local magnetization and nearest-neighbor correlations without imposing the translational symmetries of smaller unit cells.

The tensors are optimized using imaginary-time evolution with the simple-update (SU) algorithm [30]. Starting from randomly initialized tensors, we apply a sequence of local imaginary-time evolution operators,

|ψGS⟩=limβ→∞e−β​H​|ψ0⟩≃limn→∞[∏⟨i,j⟩e−τ​Hi​j]n​|ψ0⟩,|\psi_{\mathrm{GS}}\rangle=\lim_{\beta\rightarrow\infty}e^{-\beta H}|\psi_{0}\rangle\ \simeq\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left[\prod_{\langle i,j\rangle}e^{-\tau H_{ij}}\right]^{n}|\psi_{0}\rangle,

where τ\tau is the imaginary-time step and Hi​jH_{ij} denotes the local Hamiltonian acting on a nearest-neighbor bond. In practice, we gradually reduce τ\tau during the evolution. After applying each two-site gate e−τ​Hi​je^{-\tau H_{ij}}, the resulting tensors are truncated back to bond dimension DD using a singular-value decomposition. The SU procedure provides an efficient optimization of the tensors and is particularly useful for exploring the large parameter space associated with the enlarged unit cells.

After optimization, physical observables are evaluated by contracting the corresponding infinite tensor network. We use the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG) method to construct an effective environment around the tensors [40, 45]. For the kagome lattice, the contraction is formulated directly in terms of the lattice geometry, avoiding the introduction of auxiliary lattice deformations. The environment is characterized by a boundary bond dimension χ\chi, which controls the accuracy of the contraction. Observables are obtained by contracting the local tensors with this environment and are extrapolated or checked for convergence with increasing χ\chi.

For each optimized iPEPS, we increase χ\chi until the relevant observables, in particular the energy and magnetization, are converged within the required numerical accuracy. The CTMRG iterations are repeated after successive imaginary-time evolution steps so that the environment remains consistent with the evolving tensors. For the largest bond dimensions considered here, we use χ\chi values sufficiently large to ensure that the reported energies and local observables are converged with respect to the environment dimension.

For the plateau state, we analyze the local magnetization and nearest-neighbor spin-spin correlations to characterize its real-space structure.

II Further results from cluster mean-field theory

We also examine the local magnetization patterns obtained from CMFT on the nine-site cluster for the 1/91/9, 1/31/3, and 5/95/9 plateaus [Fig. S2(a)–(c)]. For the 1/91/9 plateau, we also show the corresponding spin-spin correlations in Fig. S2(d). We compare these results with the iPEPS calculations in the main text.

To further investigate the structure of the 1/91/9 magnetization plateau, we study a 27-site kagome cluster using exact diagonalization (ED). Figure S2(a) shows the lowest energies in the mz=1/2m_{z}=1/2, 3/23/2, and 5/25/2 sectors as a function of magnetic field hh. Over a finite field range, the mz=3/2m_{z}=3/2 sector has the lowest energy, corresponding to the 1/91/9 plateau.

We examine the real-space structure of this state through the local magnetization and nearest-neighbor spin-spin correlations, Ci​j=⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩C_{ij}=\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle. The resulting correlation pattern is shown in Fig. S2(b), using the same bond-color and bond-width convention as in the main text. The ED result displays a pronounced spatial modulation of the nearest-neighbor correlations.

As an independent check, we also perform cluster mean-field theory (CMFT) using the same 27-site cluster. In CMFT, the intra-cluster interactions are treated explicitly, while the coupling to neighboring clusters is decoupled at the mean-field level and determined self-consistently. The resulting nearest-neighbor correlations are shown in Fig. S2(c). The CMFT calculation reproduces the characteristic spatial modulation found in ED, demonstrating that the observed correlation pattern is robust against the treatment of the inter-cluster couplings. Both approaches therefore yield a consistent real-space structure for the 1/91/9 plateau.

III Further iPEPS results

To further characterize the 1/91/9 plateau, we examine the evolution of the local magnetizations with increasing bond dimension DD. As shown in Fig. S3, the local magnetizations exhibit no clear tendency toward the restoration of sixfold rotational symmetry. Although a reliable extrapolation to the D→∞D\to\infty limit is not possible, the observed behavior provides no clear indication that the symmetry breaking vanishes in this limit.

For comparison, we perform the same analysis for the 1/31/3 and 5/95/9 plateaus, which can be understood in terms of localized magnons on nonoverlapping hexagonal plaquettes. In these cases, the tensor-network ansatz introduces a small symmetry breaking in the local magnetizations on the hexagons hosting the localized magnons. As shown in Figs. S3 and S4, the differences between the local magnetizations decrease with increasing DD, indicating that the sixfold rotational symmetry is progressively restored in the D→∞D\to\infty limit. This behavior contrasts with that of the 1/91/9 plateau, where the local magnetizations show no analogous tendency toward symmetry restoration.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
